This duration falls within the range of 74 to 80 days reported for natural nests in the wild, though ambient fluctuations can accelerate or extend development. Upon eclosion, each hatchling possesses a modest wet body mass of roughly 42 grams [Wwb = roughly 42 grams], a value that reflects the lecithotrophic investment of the yolk-sac larva stage. The total length of these neonates at birth is consistently around 24 centimeters [Lb = around 24 centimeters], a measurement that serves as a critical baseline for quantifying subsequent growth trajectories in both field and captive studies. This initial size is considerably smaller than the dimensions attained by mature adults, highlighting the substantial ontogenetic shift in body plan that occurs over the crocodile's life span.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes pronounced as individuals approach reproductive maturity. For adult males, the ultimate total length can reach approximately 300 centimeters [Li = approximately 300 centimeters], whereas females attain a more modest asymptotic length of about 200 centimeters [Li = about 200 centimeters]. This disparity is mirrored in their ultimate wet weights, with males achieving a body mass of up to 90,000 grams (90000 grams) [Wwi = 90000 grams] and females reaching a maximum of roughly 26,600 grams (26600 grams) [Wwi = 26600 grams], a relationship consistent with the general pattern observed across other members of the Crocodylidae family. Such extreme dimorphism is ecologically significant, as larger males are better equipped to secure and defend high-quality basking and nesting territories along the river systems of northern Australia. The size advantage also influences competitive interactions during the breeding season, where larger individuals typically dominate access to gravid females.

The onset of puberty, defined here as the transition from an immature, growing juvenile to a reproductively viable organism, is associated with specific size thresholds rather than a fixed chronological age under variable field conditions. One commonly cited benchmark for this developmental milestone is a snout-to-vent length of 87 centimeters, which corresponds to a calculated total length at puberty of approximately 131 centimeters [Lp = approximately 131 centimeters]. Alternatively, a total length of 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters] is frequently used as a practical field criterion for classifying an individual as having reached sexual maturity. Accompanying these length-based definitions, the wet weight at puberty for females undergoing this transformation is estimated at roughly 7,480 grams (7480 grams) [Wwp = 7480 grams], while for males the corresponding mass is approximately 11,250 grams (11250 grams) [Wwp = 11250 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before gonadal activation can proceed.

Under a stable thermal regime of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], which represents a typical environmental condition in many of the shaded billabongs and slow-moving streams this species inhabits, the maximum reproductive rate is constrained. Field studies suggest that a female can produce roughly one egg per clutch [N_R_i = roughly one egg per clutch] with a frequency of about 13 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 13 clutches per year] when conditions are optimal and food is abundant. This relatively slow pace of reproduction, compared to many other reptiles of similar size, is likely linked to the energetic demands of constructing a large mound nest and the extended period of maternal guarding exhibited by this species. The timing of first reproduction is also mediated by temperature, with individuals maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] exhibiting a clear sexual divergence in maturation schedules. This pronounced delay in male reproductive onset is unusual among crocodilians and may reflect the intense intrasexual competition for mating opportunities, where smaller, younger males are rarely successful in securing copulations. Consequently, although males may reach the pubertal size threshold earlier, their first genuine reproductive event is deferred until they achieve a body size sufficient to contest territory ownership with larger, established rivals. This life-history strategy ultimately shapes the age structure of wild populations.
